changes.before: Replace auto b = a with auto& b = a. What prints?
changes.after: Change a copied vector without changing the original.

before: Copying a std::vector creates an independent vector with copies of its elements. auto b = a declares a new value; it is not a reference alias.
auto& b = a would make b another name for a. The ampersand changes ownership and mutation consequences. Here both indices are valid because each vector contains two elements.

Expected output or behavior: 2 9
. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Repeat with a std::string, then compare value and reference declarations. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: Copying a vector of integers creates a separate vector with copies of the integers. auto b = a creates that new vector. Later changes to b do not change a.
auto& b = a would instead make b a reference to a. Both names would then reach the same vector. The & changes whether this declaration creates a copy or another name.
The program prints 2 9. a keeps its original first value. Only the copy in b changes to nine.
A vector copy needs space and work to copy its items. Use a copy when you need an independent value. A reference can avoid that copy when sharing the original is intended.

before.question: Replace auto b = a with auto& b = a. What prints?
before.explanation: b now aliases a, so assigning b[0] changes the same element observed through a[0].

after.question: Replace auto b = a with auto& b = a. What prints?
after.explanation: b becomes another name for a. Changing b[0] changes the same item that a[0] reads.
